pairs.subject: lazy-section-addressability
pairs.evidence: app/features/insights/analytics/sections/analyticsSections.ts:8 The former long scroll was replaced by a ?sec= tab switcher that renders only the active section, so there are no named in-page locations to scroll to. A search of the sections directory (and of all of app/features/insights/analytics) found no scrollIntoView, IntersectionObserver, location.hash, getElementById or scroll-mt, which means this page has no scroll address space for the subject to govern.

techniques.evidence: app/features/insights/analytics/sections/sectionChunks.tsx:14 The code-split panels reserve height (min-h-[..rem]) but none of them is addressed by name, so no address wrapper is owed. The technique's 'locations that are not addressed' exemption applies.

app/features/insights/analytics/sections/analyticsSections.ts:14 The only published names are ?sec= values that select a whole view; there are no scroll-tracker or coaching handles to keep separate from them. The vocabulary is declared once, as the technique asks.

app/features/insights/analytics/sections/analyticsSections.ts:26 A deep link resolves to the selected section, which then renders. No jump has to wait for a section to mount on approach, so there is no scroll or retry protocol to judge.

app/features/insights/analytics/sections/analyticsSections.test.ts:23 There are no in-page anchors to cover. The nearest equivalent is a unit test over the ?sec= vocabulary: the guard, the default being a declared id, and the fallback for unknown values.

pairs.registryProposal: The subject could say outright that a query-param view switcher that renders one section at a time (rather than a long scroll) is outside its scope. A tab-addressed view is closer to app-shell routing than to scroll addressability.
